podcast.body: A "huge departure" from previous material, this song was based on Tony Martin's 1950 hit "There's No Tomorrow," which in turn derived from the public domain song "O Sole Mio." Freddie Bienstock of Hill & Range commissioned new lyrics for it. Despite an engineer's suggestion to splice takes, Elvis insisted on performing the difficult, sustained final note all the way through, resulting in an "extraordinary" performance unlike any he'd given before, and it went to number one. It was the only song the Colonel ever specifically asked Elvis to record. "Elvis did several near perfect takes of the song, but then kept flubbing the ending, which required a particularly powerful sustained note."

podcast.body: This song is cited as another example of how an Elvis Presley 45 rpm single could easily debut at number one on the British charts due to their sales-only methodology. If enough copies were sold in a week, the song could directly reach the top spot, unlike the more complex US Hot 100 which also included radio airplay. "That's what made it easier for songs like Elvis Presley's Jail House Rock or it's now or never to enter the British charts at number one."
